---
title: Language Server Development
description: >-
  How the Panache language server works: incremental document synchronization,
  parsing, and the LSP features it implements.
---

### Document Synchronization

The LSP tracks document changes using **incremental synchronization**:

`textDocument/didOpen`
:   Document opened in editor

`textDocument/didChange`
:   Document content changed (incremental deltas sent)

`textDocument/didClose`
:   Document closed

This ensures the LSP always has the current document state while minimizing data
transfer.

### One Tree, Derived on Demand

The notification handlers write salsa *inputs* only --- they never parse. Every
consumer (request handlers, the linter, diagnostics) reads the tree from the
`parsed_document` query, so there is exactly one parse of a document per
revision and no way for a handler to see a tree that disagrees with the text it
was handed.

`parsed_document` splices that tree off the previous parse instead of reparsing
from scratch, which is the default; `PANACHE_INCREMENTAL_PARSING=0` turns it off
for debugging, as does the deprecated `experimental.incrementalParsing = false`
client setting. The previous parse lives in a side channel beside salsa
(`src/incremental.rs`), keyed on `(file, config)` and reused only when both the
config value and the document's reference-definition set are unchanged ---
retained blocks keep the resolution and options they were parsed with, so either
changing invalidates them at a distance.

The splice is attempted in four tiers, cheapest first, and the first one that
succeeds wins:

- **Token.** An edit strictly inside one plain-prose `TEXT` token of a top-level
  paragraph replaces that one green token. It costs the token's length plus a
  green root rebuild, so like the region tier below and unlike the two windows
  it does not scale with the document --- which is what makes a keystroke in a
  300 KB file cost what a keystroke in a small one does. It is tried before the
  cost guards below, so an accepted edit also skips the price of deciding not to
  reuse. The guards are strict: the edit must not touch either end of the
  token's non-whitespace core, every byte of the token must be inert prose, the
  token must still read as one `TEXT` on its own, and the edit must sit past its
  line's first word so no block marker can be manufactured.
- **Region.** Re-parses one contiguous run of top-level `DOCUMENT` children ---
  the run the edit touches, widened until a blank line sits on each side. Unlike
  the two below it, the parse is *bounded*: it covers the region and not the
  rest of the document, so an edit near the top of a large file costs what the
  same edit costs near the bottom. It answers most edits in ordinary prose
  documents.
- **Section window.** Re-parses from the previous top-level heading, and
  re-adopts the old tail by `Arc` identity when it comes back structurally
  equal.
- **Suffix window.** Re-parses from the enclosing block.

The two window tiers parse to the end of the document. The region tier does not,
and the difference is not that bounded parsing turned out to be safe after all ---
a fragment parsed on its own really is untrustworthy, because list-item
buffering, fence pairing and table detection all depend on lookahead that runs
past the fragment's end. It is that the fragment is never trusted on its own.
Each seam is proved by re-parsing the fragment together with the one neighbour
on that side and requiring three things: that no top-level child straddles the
seam, that the fragment comes back with exactly the children and errors it
produced in isolation, and that the neighbour comes back byte-identical.
Anything the fragment leaves open --- an unclosed fence or div --- swallows
greedily, so it reaches that neighbour first and cannot hide.

Two constructs reach further than one neighbour and no boundary parse can catch
them: a fence can pair with an opener several blocks back (under the Pandoc
dialect an *unclosed* fence is ordinary paragraph text, so the opener looks
inert), and a multiline-table border pairs across arbitrarily many
blank-line-separated blocks. The region tier answers those by comparing the
region's delimiter lines before and after the edit: if they are unchanged, the
document's whole sequence of them is unchanged, so no pairing anywhere can move.
That admits editing prose, a table cell, or a code block's body, and declines an
edit that adds, removes, or alters a delimiter.

All four tiers stay because all four are used. Over the fuzzer's real-document
corpus, the region tier takes about three quarters of splices, the section
window a seventh, and the suffix window and token tier the rest; on heading-less
documents the suffix window becomes the workhorse instead.
`crates/panache-parser/tests/incremental_fuzz.rs` prints that histogram on every
run.

Four properties make reading and writing that channel from inside an otherwise
pure query sound:

- A successful splice is byte-identical to a full parse, tree *and* syntax
  errors. The parser asserts this on every splice in debug builds; setting
  `PANACHE_REPARSE_ORACLE=1` adds a second check against a real full parse
  before anything is stored. Both oracles cost a full parse each, so both are
  compiled out of release builds; what survives there is the one part of the
  invariant that is `O(1)` --- the spliced tree spans exactly the text it was
  spliced from. That check runs in every build and *falls back* to a full parse
  rather than panicking, because `parsed_document` feeds formatting, which
  writes the user's file.
- Every guard declines to `None` rather than guessing, so the query's fallback
  is an ordinary full parse.
- Two guards decline for cost rather than correctness, one per tier that has a
  cost worth guarding. Both *window* strategies parse their window to the end of
  the document, so a window that starts near the top of the file re-derives
  nearly all of it and then pays a splice on top: measured, that is a 5-10% loss
  against simply parsing the file again, so a window leaving more than 85% of
  the document downstream is refused. The *region* tier answers a region with a
  fragment parse plus up to two neighbour-sized boundary parses --- roughly
  three region-sized parses --- so a region covering more than a quarter of the
  document is refused for the same reason, counting its neighbours as well as
  itself. Both are evaluated before any parse runs, and a whole-document
  replacement (which some clients send on every format-on-save) fails both and
  costs the full parse it would have cost anyway. `benches/lsp_incremental.rs`
  carries the measurements and a case on each side of both thresholds.
- The base is stored last, after every fallible step, so a panic or a salsa
  cancellation mid-query can never leave a base whose text and tree disagree.
  Stores are not ordered across revisions, so an older base can overwrite a
  newer one; each is internally consistent, and a stale base only widens the
  next diff.

Only the LSP admits a document to the channel, and only while the setting is on ---
which it is unless a client or `PANACHE_INCREMENTAL_PARSING=0` says otherwise.
Switched off, nothing is admitted, so every parse is a full parse.

### Durability and Invalidation Policy

Panache uses Salsa durability levels to reduce unnecessary revalidation work in
LSP mode.

#### Durability assignments

`LOW`
:   Open-buffer text updates (`didOpen`, `didChange`) for the active document.

`MEDIUM`
:   Per-document config updates and file-watcher refreshes for already cached
    dependency files.

`HIGH`
:   Disk-loaded dependency files cached from the project graph.

#### Invalidation policy

- Edits while typing should invalidate low-durability data aggressively, but
  should not force broad revalidation of stable dependency data.
- Config reloads and watcher events use medium durability so changes propagate,
  but with less churn than open-buffer edits.
- Disk-cached dependencies use high durability so unrelated low-frequency edits
  do not repeatedly revalidate those inputs.

#### Verification and measurement

- Durability revalidation measurement harness: `tests/durability_bench.rs`
  (ignored by default).

- Run with:

  ```bash
  cargo test --test durability_bench durability_revalidation_bench -- --ignored --nocapture
  ```

- Policy regression tests are in `src/salsa.rs` and validate that
  high-durability stable inputs avoid revalidation under low-durability updates,
  while low-durability stable inputs are revalidated.
